items.title: [SECURITY]: Compaction summary injects actionable instructions — model executes without user consent
items.body:
### Description

### Description

When opencode auto-compacts a long conversation, the compaction summary can contain a "Next Move" or action plan section. The model treats this summary as user input and executes on the prescribed actions without asking the user. This is an instruction injection vector that bypasses the normal user-in-the-loop safety model.

### Model Used
Big Pickle

### Reproduction

1. Work in a long session with tools configured (MCP servers, bash, file editing, etc.)
2. Context fills up → opencode triggers auto-compaction
3. Compaction summary includes a "Next Move" section with suggested next steps
4. After compaction, the model immediately executes on those suggestions without user confirmation
5. In the observed case, this included attempting SSH connections to remote servers

### What happened (observed twice)

First occurrence:
- Auto-compaction initiated at 67% usage after model read and accessed opencode documentation
- Auto-compaction injected a "Next Move" section
- Model treated it as user instructions
- Executed on suggested actions without asking

Second occurrence (more severe):
- Auto-compaction injected a "Next Move" section listing 6+ actions
- Model immediately began executing — including attempting SSH connections to a remote server
- The SSH attempts used ssh-keyscan, and ssh -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no — all without the user requesting any of this nor had user ever asked the model to ever make use of SSH in the past
- User had to intervene to stop the behavior

### Why this is a security issue

1. Instruction injection vector: The compaction summary effectively becomes a prompt injection channel. Anything embedded in the summary (including data from tool outputs, MCP responses, or web fetches) can become "instructions" the model follows.

2. Bypasses user consent: The model treats compaction-injected suggestions as if the user said them. Actions are taken without explicit approval.

3. Escalation risk: In the observed case, the model attempted SSH connections to remote servers that the user never had the model make before. In other scenarios, this could lead to unauthorized file modifications, API calls, or data exposure.

4. Trust boundary violation: The compaction system is supposed to summarize context, not prescribe actions. The model cannot distinguish between "user said this" and "compaction summary said this."

### Environment

- opencode version: current (as of July 2026)
- model: Big Pickle

### Plugins

None

### OpenCode version

1.17.18

### Steps to reproduce

1. Work in a long session with tools configured (MCP servers, bash, file editing, etc.)
2. Context fills up → opencode triggers auto-compaction
3. Compaction summary includes a "Next Move" section with suggested next steps
4. After compaction, the model immediately executes on those suggestions without user confirmation
5. In the observed case, this included attempting SSH connections to remote servers

### Screenshot and/or share link

_No response_

### Operating System

Debian 13

### Terminal

xfce4-terminal

items.title: [FEATURE]: Return OpenCode Go usage with each response and keep it on the message
items.body:
### Feature hasn't been suggested before.

- [x] I have verified this feature I'm about to request hasn't been suggested before.

### Describe the enhancement you want to request

There is no way to see OpenCode Go usage from inside OpenCode; you have to open the console. #25875 and #27698 asked for it in the TUI. The usage endpoint from #16513 exists, but nothing in OpenCode uses it.

Proposal: the gateway already loads the Go usage on every request to check the limits, and already adds a `cost` field to each response (a `ping` chunk with `cost` at the end of streams). It could add the same `{ rolling, weekly, monthly }` object that `/zen/go/v1/usage` returns, for example:

```json
{ "type": "ping", "cost": "0", "goUsage": {
  "rolling": { "status": "ok", "percent": 62, "resetsAt": "2026-10-06T10:15:00Z" },
  "weekly":  { "status": "ok", "percent": 81, "resetsAt": "2026-10-12T00:00:00Z" },
  "monthly": { "status": "ok", "percent": 37, "resetsAt": "2026-10-18T03:20:00Z" } } }
```

OpenCode would then store it on the assistant message, next to tokens and cost.

What this gives:

- The TUI can show Go usage (sidebar or footer) and keep it current without any extra request.
- Nothing has to poll `/zen/go/v1/usage`. Status bars and tray apps can read the last value from the local database instead of calling the API with the user's key, the same way Codex writes `rate_limits` into its session log.
- The key never leaves OpenCode.

The value only changes when Go is used through OpenCode, but `resetsAt` lets a reader handle resets without asking the server.

Context: I maintain a Windows tray app that shows plan usage for several coding tools. It only reads what the tools themselves record or report and never handles credentials, so today it can't support Go.

If you'd want the server side, I'm happy to send the client side (reading the field and storing it on the message). A smaller alternative would be an `opencode usage --format json` command over the existing endpoint.

Prior: #9281 and #40584 (closed), #32913 (CLI command plus endpoint, now conflicts with #16513), #41824 (exposing Go usage through the OpenCode server, closed by the PR cleanup).

items.title: Doom-loop detection misses periodic tool-call cycles
items.body:
### Description

The `doom_loop` guard detects three adjacent identical tool calls, but misses alternating calls such as `A, B, A, B, A, B`. Repeating the same multi-call block never satisfies the current last-three-parts comparison.

I reproduced this with a deterministic normalized stream driving the real `SessionProcessor`, without changing production code. The period-2 regression fails because processing returns `continue` without asking permission. A period-1 control (`A, A, A`, with distinct call IDs) passes.

### Plugins

None in the reproduction fixture.

### OpenCode version

Upstream `dev` at `57ef3828431790c53f8f333c7ffbfe88770a1812`.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Configure `doom_loop: "ask"` and create a fresh assistant processor.
2. Supply a normalized stream with `step-start`, followed by these calls in order. Give every call a unique ID and follow each with a successful `tool-result`:

   ```text
   lookup({query: "a"})  call-a1
   search({query: "b"})  call-b1
   lookup({query: "a"})  call-a2
   search({query: "b"})  call-b2
   lookup({query: "a"})  call-a3
   search({query: "b"})  call-b3
   ```

3. End with `step-finish(tool-calls)` and `finish(tool-calls)`.
4. Observe six completed tool parts, no `permission.asked` event, and processor result `continue`.

Expected: three complete repetitions of this two-call block should reach the existing `doom_loop` permission gate, just as three repetitions of a single call do.

This is distinct from #46272's consecutive-identical-call stop threshold and #32089's cross-message history scan. The sequence above occurs entirely within one active processor. It does not require changing permission actions or adding an unconditional stop.

### Operating System

Linux. Reproduced in the processor Effect test suite, without an external provider.

items.title: core: permission "ask" silently auto-approved — no request created (deny still enforced)
items.body:
### Description

Rules resolving to "ask" are silently auto-approved by the shared background service. The tool call just runs: no permission request is created, the session permission queue stays empty, and no permission.* events appear in the server log (other bus event types are logged normally). deny rules in the same permissions array ARE enforced before execution — so the rules are evaluated; only the ask branch proceeds without asking. Net effect equals --auto mode even though --auto is set nowhere.

Not client-specific: the TUI (no --auto in argv, no auto indicator visible) and fresh opencode run sessions both execute silently. Third-party integrator reports (open-design#7624) describe opencode run stopping at permission prompts — ours never prompts. Not shell-specific either: the base external_directory ask is bypassed too (agent read /etc/hosts with no prompt).

Ruled out locally: saved approvals empty; session permission DB column NULL; no OPENCODE_* env vars on TUI or service processes; no launchd-registered flags; plugins (opencode-mem, superpowers) inspected — neither registers a permission.evaluate handler; forcing OPENCODE_CLI_CONFIG_CONTENT with session.permissions=prompt changed nothing; identical behavior with the old V1 permission.bash syntax; full service restart re-reads config (GET /api/config shows the array intact with effect ask) and changes nothing. Reproducible 100%.

Expected: per docs, ask means "wait for a decision from the client". Actual: behaves as if auto-approval were always on. Security-relevant: ask guardrails for rm/cp/mv/sed and .env/external-directory access do nothing in the default mode.

### Plugins

_No response_

### OpenCode version

2.0.29 (channel: latest)

### Steps to reproduce

1. Global config ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json (plus any working provider/model):
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "permissions": [
    { "action": "read",  "resource": "*",             "effect": "allow" },
    { "action": "shell", "resource": "*",             "effect": "allow" },
    { "action": "shell", "resource": "mv *",          "effect": "ask" },
    { "action": "shell", "resource": "cp *",          "effect": "ask" },
    { "action": "shell", "resource": "rm *",          "effect": "ask" },
    { "action": "shell", "resource": "rm -rf *",      "effect": "deny" },
    { "action": "shell", "resource": "sudo rm -rf *", "effect": "deny" }
  ]
}

2. Confirm parse: opencode api get "/api/config?location%5Bdirectory%5D=$PWD" -> the global document shows the array above, effect "ask" intact.
3. 3. Fresh TUI session, agent runs: cp a b -> executes immediately, no dialog. GET /api/session/<id>/permission -> {"data":[]}.
4. 4. Control (proves rules are evaluated): agent runs mkdir d && rm -rf d -> blocked before execution, tool result {"error":{"type":"permission.rejected","message":"Permission denied: shell"}} — the mkdir never ran either.
5. 5. Control (client-independent): fresh shell, opencode run with prompt "execute exactly: cp x y" and NO --auto -> executes silently, y created, exit 0.
6. 6. Control (not shell-specific): agent reads external path /etc/hosts -> no config rule touches external_directory, base policy asks -> silent success.
7. 7. Control (client setting): OPENCODE_CLI_CONFIG_CONTENT='{"session":{"permissions":"prompt"}}' opencode run "execute mv a b" -> still silent.

### Screenshot and/or share link

_No response_

### Operating System

macOS (Darwin 27.0.0, arm64)

### Terminal

Tabby (TERM_PROGRAM=Tabby) inside /bin/zsh

items.title: [FEATURE]: Expose OPENCODE_SESSION_ID to the AI agent subprocess env for self-identification
items.body:
### Feature hasn't been suggested before.

- [x] I have verified this feature I'm about to request hasn't been suggested before. *(This request is scoped to the **agent-host subprocess** — the process running the LLM agent itself — which #15739 / #51975 explicitly do not cover; see "Relation to prior issues" below.)*

### Describe the enhancement you want to request

AI agents spawned by opencode currently have no reliable way to learn **which opencode session they belong to**. This matters for:

1. **Audit trails** — agents writing session provenance into project docs / commit messages ("which session produced this change?").
2. **Multi-session disambiguation** — several opencode sessions can run against the same project directory concurrently (main session + subagents). Today an agent can only guess by querying `~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db` (the `session` table, roughly `WHERE directory = <cwd> ORDER BY time_updated DESC LIMIT 1`) — which returns the **latest** row, not necessarily the caller's session. Under same-directory concurrency this is silently wrong.
3. **Attribution** — anything an agent reports about "this session" is unverifiable without asking the user to quit opencode and copy the `Continue  opencode -s <id>` line from the terminal.

Environment observed in the **agent-host subprocess** (opencode 1.18.34, Windows, verified 2026-10-03): `OPENCODE`, `OPENCODE_BIN_PATH`, `OPENCODE_CLIENT`, `OPENCODE_CONFIG`, `OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT`, `OPENCODE_DB`, `OPENCODE_DISABLE_CLAUDE_CODE_PROMPT`, `OPENCODE_PID` — but **no session identifier**.

### Relation to prior issues (and why this is not a duplicate)

- #15739 (closed as completed via #51975) solved this for **shell-tool subprocesses**: commands executed through the bash/agent's tool interface now receive `OPENCODE_SESSION_ID`. That surface is explicitly *not* the one this request covers.
- #9292 / #12158 / #40255 likewise discuss tool/shell/MCP child environments.

**The uncovered surface**: the process opencode spawns to *host the agent itself* (the one whose env the agent can inspect directly, and from which user-configured scripts/hooks/agents may run) still receives no session identifier. Concretely: an agent that wants to self-identify *without* going through a tool-exec round-trip — or scripts run by harness integrations outside the tool-exec path — have no exact signal, only DB heuristics that are ambiguous under same-directory concurrency.

**Suggested implementation**: inject the same variable into the agent-host subprocess at spawn time:

```
OPENCODE_SESSION_ID=sess_xxx
```

This is the same variable already shipped for tool subprocesses in #51975, so the two surfaces stay consistent and consumers can use one name everywhere.

### Current workaround

We run a best-effort detector (a small script agents invoke at session start) that:

- reads the `session` table filtered by `directory` (normalized cwd match),
- applies an activity window and **explicit degradation** when ≥2 sessions are active in the same directory (`same-dir concurrency` → refuse to answer rather than guess),
- falls through stale / no-row states with honest `unknown` semantics (never a confident wrong id),
- has an env-first branch reserved: as soon as `OPENCODE_SESSION_ID` reaches this surface, it switches over with zero consumer changes.

Same-directory concurrency is fundamentally ambiguous from outside the process tree — the env var at spawn time is the only *exact* solution, and opencode already holds the truth there.

- opencode version: 1.18.34
- OS: Windows 11

items.title: Critical: Agent ran destructive InfluxDB command without user approval, causing data loss
items.body:
### Description

Summary
The opencode agent executed DROP MEASUREMENT govee_temperature against a live InfluxDB database without user approval, permanently deleting all temperature data across all retention policies. This was a catastrophic error during a dashboard editing task.

What happened
User asked to edit a Home Assistant dashboard (Govee T&H) to add average temperature lines and change humidity retention from 15 to 366 days.
Agent successfully modified the custom card JS and dashboard config.
Agent discovered that InfluxDB continuous queries needed updating to support the changes.
Agent connected to InfluxDB at local-govee-influxdb:8086 and created new CQs — this was reasonable.
Critical error: Agent then ran DROP MEASUREMENT govee_temperature intending to re-backfill temperature data with mean values. This deleted ALL temperature data from ALL retention policies (raw_3h, hourly_366d, hourly_15d).
Impact
All historical temperature data for 11 rooms permanently destroyed
Data was migrated from HA Recorder to InfluxDB at a cost of ~$20 in AI fees
No backup exists of the InfluxDB data
Humidity data was unaffected
Root cause
The agent used a destructive database command (DROP MEASUREMENT) without:

Asking the user for approval
Verifying the scope of the deletion (it affects ALL retention policies, not just one)
Considering safer alternatives (e.g., writing a new measurement, or accepting None values for historical mean)
What should have happened
Agent should have asked user approval before any database mutation
Agent should have used a non-destructive approach (e.g., accept None mean for historical data, or write to a new measurement)
Agent should never have run DROP MEASUREMENT on a production database
Suggested improvements
Add explicit user confirmation before any destructive database operations (DROP, DELETE)
Treat InfluxDB and other database systems as read-only unless user explicitly approves writes
Add a safety check that warns when a command will affect more data than expected
Log all database mutations for audit purposes
Affected user
Contact: [opencode@rick-leslie.name](mailto:opencode@rick-leslie.name)

### Plugins

Opencode, InfluxDB

### OpenCode version

2.5.3

### Steps to reproduce

Ask Opencode to a question without giving any instruction to do anything. It just goes on to perform tasks that it has not been asked to perform, including destructive actions.

### Screenshot and/or share link

Nothing to show

### Operating System

Home Assistant 

### Terminal

Home Assistant

items.title: feat(app): per-project auto-accept permissions overriding a default
items.body: ## Summary After #44608, auto-accept permissions became one app-wide switch. This PR keeps that switch as the **default** and adds a per-project override in **project settings**. - **Settings → Preferences → Auto-accept permissions** (switch): the default for every project. Copy: "Approve permission requests without asking. Projects can override this in their settings." - **Settings → Projects → (project) → Auto-accept permissions** (dropdown): **Use default (On/Off)** / **On** / **Off**. Copy: "Approve this project's permission requests without asking". A project uses its own choice when it has one and the default otherwise, so it can opt in while the default is off, or opt out while it's on. ### Details - Overrides are keyed by server scope + project ID, since project IDs are only unique per server. They're stored in `settings.v3` as `permissions.autoApproveProjects`; a project with no entry uses the default. Existing `autoApprove: true` users keep their default on. - From a session, the `mod+shift+a` command now sets the current project's choice. If the new value matches the default, the project goes back to using the default. Copy: "Auto-accept permissions for this project", toast "Auto-accepting permissions for this project". - The per-server auto-approver replies only for covered projects. For a request from a session the client hasn't loaded, it fetches the session first to find its project. Permission docks and tab attention dots are hidden only for covered projects. ## Tests - `bun run typecheck` (packages/app) - `bun run test:unit` (packages/app): 749 pass - Playwright on this branch, `settings`, `settings-search`, `session-request-docks`, `multi-server` and `command-palette`: 60 pass - New `multi-server` case: with the default off, setting a project to On approves only that project's request. A project set to Off keeps prompting after the default turns on, then is approved once it goes back to "Use default (On)". The case fails if the approver ignores project overrides. Requested by: @Brendonovich (Brendan via Slack)

items.title: [FEATURE][Desktop]: Show a persistent indicator when auto-accept permissions is active, and make the setting a real default for new sessions
items.body:
### Describe the enhancement you want to request

**Problem**

Since v1.4.0 (#23586), auto-accept permissions is toggled via Settings → General or the command palette (`Cmd+Shift+A`), but once enabled there is **no persistent visual indication** in the session UI that subsequent tool calls run without approval. The only feedback is a one-time toast. This leads to two issues:

1. **Safety / awareness.** There is no way to tell at a glance that the current session auto-approves permission requests — for example after toggling it via the keybind by accident, or when returning to a session started earlier. Other agent harnesses address this with a persistent status indicator (e.g. Claude Code shows its "bypass permissions" mode in the status line).
2. **Confusing persistence.** As noted in #25642, the Settings toggle looks like a global preference but effectively resets for new sessions, because toggling it inside a session is session-scoped. Users who want auto-accept as their default workflow have to re-enable it constantly.

**Relation to previous requests**

I'm aware of #21578, #25642 and #21423 (closed as not planned), which asked to restore the per-session toggle button in the session UI. This request is deliberately different: it does **not** ask to bring back per-session controls, and keeps the v1.4.0 design direction. It only asks to (a) surface the *already tracked* auto-accept state and (b) make the *already existing* setting behave predictably.

**Proposal**

1. **Persistent indicator while auto-accept is active.** A small badge in the prompt footer, next to the model/variant selector — e.g. `⚡ Auto-accept` (icon + short label, distinct styling, tooltip: "Permission requests are being auto-approved"). The state is already available (`permission.isAutoAccepting(sessionID, directory)` / `isAutoAcceptingDirectory`), so this is a read-only visualization of existing state with no changes to permission logic. Optionally, clicking the badge could disable auto-accept or explain how to turn it off.
2. **Make the Settings toggle an honest default for new sessions.** When auto-accept is enabled globally (Settings → General, outside a session), persist it so that new sessions start with auto-accept on until it is explicitly disabled. This matches the mechanism already used for `permission: "allow"` in config (`enableConfiguredDirectory`) and resolves the confusion described in #25642 — without adding any new controls to the session UI.

The two parts complement each other: a persistent default is only good UX when its state is constantly visible — which is exactly what the indicator provides.

**Benefits**

- Users always know when OpenCode acts without asking — fewer "surprise" approvals. Related: #15589, where auto-accept re-enabling unexpectedly was reported as a bug; a visible indicator makes such behavior immediately explainable.
- Power users get a stable "auto-accept by default" workflow without re-toggling every session.
- No regression of the v1.4.0 simplification: zero new per-session controls, just one small read-only badge.
- Better discoverability of the feature for new users.

**Environment**

OpenCode Desktop 1.18.4, macOS

items.title: Skill name collisions are resolved non-deterministically (last file read wins), so a project skill can take over a configured skill and its `permission.skill` allow rule
items.body:
### Description

**Version:** 1.18.30 and 1.18.34 (linux-x64), the loader code is identical in both

### What happens

When two skills declare the same `name:`, which one OpenCode uses depends on timing. The skill loader reads all discovered `SKILL.md` files concurrently (`forEach(..., { concurrency: "unbounded" })`) and stores each one in a map keyed by name. On a duplicate it logs `duplicate skill name` but still overwrites the entry, so the file whose read finishes last wins.

Usually that is the skill from `skills.paths`, because it is discovered last. Under load the order sometimes flips.

### Why it matters

We allow curated skills by name and ask for everything else:

```jsonc
"skills": { "paths": ["/etc/opencode/skills"] },
"permission": { "skill": { "*": "ask", "team-skill": "allow" } }
```

A repository that ships `.opencode/skills/<anything>/SKILL.md` with `name: team-skill` sometimes replaces the curated skill. It is then loaded under the `allow` rule, without asking. Project skills cannot be disabled on their own: `OPENCODE_DISABLE_PROJECT_CONFIG` also drops the project's `AGENTS.md`. So a name-based allow rule cannot reliably protect curated skills.

### Reproduction

1. Put a skill with `name: team-skill` into the `skills.paths` directory.
2. Put a second skill with the same name into the project at `.opencode/skills/x/SKILL.md`.
3. Run `opencode debug skill` in parallel, for example 8 at a time, and look at the `location` of `team-skill`.

In our runs the project copy won about 1 in 200 queries under that load, and 0 of 36 when run one after another.

### Expected

Precedence should be deterministic and documented. For example, configured `skills.paths` and the global config win over project skills, or a duplicate name is an error. At minimum, the result should not depend on read timing.

Once all files are read, assigning the matches in discovery order would make it deterministic.

### Plugins

_No response_

### OpenCode version

1.18.34

### Steps to reproduce

_No response_

### Screenshot and/or share link

### Operating System

WSL2 with Ubuntu 26.04

items.title: feat(acp): support additional workspace directories
items.body:
[#35457](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/issues/35457)

## Why the change

ACP clients can now give a session extra workspace roots with `additionalDirectories`, and opencode tools can work in those roots without asking for outside-directory approval each time.

## Special things to note

- The session metadata key `opencode.acp.additionalDirectories` is the source of truth. Rules are derived from it, and a session rule is ACP's only if it exactly equals a rule derived from the stored list. Load, resume and fork replace those rules and keep every other rule and metadata key. Each root is granted under both its written spelling and its real path, because tools compare paths without following symlinks.
- Grants persist on the server session. They also apply when the session is used from the TUI, and child sessions copy them when they are created, so a child created earlier keeps roots its parent later dropped. Session rules are checked after config rules, so a config `external_directory` deny inside a granted root is overridden. `read`, `edit` and shell rules still apply.
- Entries must be absolute and must not contain `*` or `?`, because the permission matcher has no escaping. Anything else is rejected with `-32602`. The ACP SDK (1.2.1) silently drops entries that are not strings and turns a value that is not an array into `[]` before the agent sees it, which fails toward a smaller scope. Discovery, the Location root, and telling the model about the roots are deferred core work.

## Change outline

Each lifecycle request maps to a session change through the existing session API:

```diff
 session/new      { cwd, additionalDirectories }
+  parse → session.create({ location, permissions: rules(dirs), metadata: { [key]: dirs } })   # no field → neither
 session/load     { sessionId, cwd, additionalDirectories }
 session/resume   { sessionId, cwd, additionalDirectories }
+  parse → getSession → activate(session, dirs) → attach
 session/fork     { sessionId, cwd, additionalDirectories }
+  parse → fork → activate(forked, dirs)        # forks copy rules and metadata, so inherited grants are replaced
 session/list
+  SessionInfo.additionalDirectories = metadata[key]
 initialize
+  sessionCapabilities.additionalDirectories = {}
```

How a root becomes rules and how `activate` reconciles them:

```ts
// parse: path.resolve without following symlinks; drop duplicates and roots whose real path is cwd's
"/tmp/shared" → [
  { action: "external_directory", resource: "/tmp/shared/*", effect: "allow" },
  { action: "external_directory", resource: "/private/tmp/shared/*", effect: "allow" }, // real path, when different
]

// activate: one PATCH, only for the fields that changed
owned       = rules(metadata[key])
permissions = [...rules(dirs), ...session.permissions.filter((rule) => !owned.includes(rule))]
metadata    = { ...session.metadata without key, ...(dirs.length ? { [key]: dirs } : {}) }
```

ACP rules go first so the session's other rules, including denies, keep precedence for the same paths. `FileAccess` asks for `<parent dir>/*` on any path outside the session directory. Core takes the last rule that matches, and `*` in a pattern also matches `/`. So `/abs/root/*` allows anything under the root, but not `/abs/rootx/*` or `/abs/*`.

items.title: fix(acp): settle permissions replied elsewhere and type request failures
items.body:
## Why the change

ACP left stale permission prompts open when core settled them, and several request failures reached the client as "Internal service failure" defects instead of typed errors.

## Special things to note

- Core publishes `permission.replied` for every request it settles. That includes a `reject` that settles the whole session, an `always` rule that now allows other asks, and a reply from another client. ACP now withdraws the client request and skips its own reply. A late reply that still races the settle gets `PermissionNotFoundError`, which is now ignored like the form equivalents.
- Permissions and forms now share one settle path: one set of asked IDs, one `settled` map, one `AskSettled` output. Permission and form IDs have distinct prefixes, so one key space is safe.
- We advertise `mcpCapabilities.sse: false`, so SSE servers are now rejected along with `type: "acp"`, instead of being accepted as remote.

## Change outline

Permissions and forms now settle the same way.

```diff
 step(state, event)
   permission.asked    -> PermissionAsk, add ID to state.asks
   form.created        -> FormAsk, add ID to state.asks
-  form.replied/cancel -> FormSettled
+  permission.replied  ┐
+  form.replied/cancel ┴-> AskSettled { id }, if state.asks has it

 ACPPermission.reply
-  race(cancelled -> "reject", ask(client))
+  race(cancelled -> "reject", settled -> "settled", ask(client))
+  "settled" cancels the client request and sends no server reply
+  PermissionNotFoundError from the server reply is ignored
```

The remaining fixes are small and local.

```diff
 service.ts
+  new / load / resume / fork: reject `acp` and `sse` MCP servers with -32602 before any server call
-  load failure: sessions.detach(id)
+  load failure: sessions.release(attached)   # no-op once re-attached
 client.ts
+  InvalidCursorError -> InvalidRequestError (field: cursor)
 agent.ts
-  ACPCatalogNotReadyError -> defect, "Internal service failure"
+  ACPCatalogNotReadyError -> ServiceFailureError("No models are available", errorName: CatalogNotReady)
 permission.ts
-  applyPatch throws -> defect -> auto "reject" without asking
+  applyPatch throws -> no preview, the ask still goes ahead
 turn.ts
-  Ref.get + Ref.set per event
+  Ref.modify per event
-  windDown returns once the drain ends
+  windDown returns only when the drain succeeds, or else abandons open tools
 turn.ts, catalog.ts, sessions.ts
-  silent ignoreCause on event streams, interrupt, child notification, usage update
+  log a warning on failure, stay quiet on interrupt
```

Tests:

- `permission.test.ts`: three asks, and the server settles the first two with `permission.replied`. The first client request gets `$/cancel_request`, the queued one is never shown, and no reply is sent for either. The third is answered, the prompt ends with `end_turn`, and nothing is logged.
- `session.test.ts`: `session/new` with an ACP or SSE MCP server, and `session/load` with an ACP one, return `-32602`. No session is created and no server call is made.
- `error.test.ts`: the event stream test now checks exact logs per row. A clean end logs nothing. A dropped connection logs exactly the two event stream failures. `wire-fixture.ts` captures logs again so tests can assert this.

items.title: fix(core): explain unanalyzable shell commands
items.body:
## Why

When the portable shell scanner can't analyze a command, the shell tool refuses it with only a reason code:

```
Portable shell scanner cannot analyze command: command-substitution
```

Agents most often hit this when they put Markdown in a double-quoted argument, for example ``note add --body "uses `vec3(1.0)` here" Title``. Bash treats those backticks as command substitution and would try to run `vec3(1.0)` as a command. Refusing is correct, but the error doesn't explain what went wrong or how to fix it, so agents keep retrying variations or give up.

## What Changes

The scanner still refuses commands it can't analyze, and they still never run. The error now says the command was not run, keeps the reason code, and explains how to rewrite the command.

**Before**

```
Portable shell scanner cannot analyze command: command-substitution
```

**After**

```
Command was not run: the shell permission scanner cannot analyze it (command-substitution). A command substitution or nested expansion is incomplete or cannot be checked. Inside double quotes, the shell runs text between backticks as a command. For literal backticks, such as Markdown code spans, use single quotes, escape each backtick as \`, or write the text to a file and pass "$(cat file)". Rewrite the command and try again.
```

Every `OpaqueReason` now has its own hint, such as "A quote is not closed." or "A redirection is missing its target or is not allowed here."

| Command | Result |
| --- | --- |
| ``note add --body "uses `vec3(1.0)` here" T`` | Not run. The error explains how to pass literal backticks |
| ``note add --body 'uses `vec3(1.0)` here' T`` | Runs. The backticks stay literal |
| `note add --body "$(cat notes.md)" T` | Runs. `note add …` and `cat notes.md` are checked as separate resources |
| `note add --body "$(cat notes.md)" T` with `cat *` denied | Blocked by the deny rule |

## Permission Safety

I chose not to fall back to asking for approval. The default policy allows every `shell` resource, so a whole-command fallback resource would be auto-allowed. That would let commands inside an unanalyzed substitution get past deny rules like `cat *` or `rm *`. The permissions docs also say tree-sitter is not a fallback and that there is no extra approval mode. This PR leaves those rules unchanged and updates the docs to describe the clearer error and how substitutions are checked.

## Scope

This PR changes only the scanner's error messages, adds tests and updates the docs. Adding a forced-approval fallback for unanalyzable commands would need a new Permission mode that ignores allow rules. That belongs in its own PR if we want it.

## Verification

```shell
cd packages/core
bun run test test/shell-parse.test.ts test/shell-parse-parity.test.ts
bun run test test/tool-shell.test.ts
bun run test test/shell-scan test/shell-parse-compatibility.test.ts test/shell-parse-syntax.test.ts test/permission.test.ts
bun run typecheck
```

- Shell parse and parity tests: 62 passed.
- `tool-shell.test.ts`: 93 passed, 19 skipped (Windows and PowerShell). New end-to-end tests use the real Permission service and a real `sh`:
  - `printf '%s' "$(cat body.md)"` reproduces a Markdown file containing backticks byte for byte.
  - A `cat *` deny rule blocks the same command, and its marker file is never written.
  - A double-quoted `` `vec3(1.0)` `` returns the new message without running or asking for permission. The single-quoted rewrite runs.
- Scanner, compatibility, syntax and permission tests: 3415 passed, 5 skipped.
- Typecheck passed.

items.title: perf(desktop): boot the renderer alongside the main bundle
items.body:
Bottom of a 7-PR stack that gets the desktop window from "visible" to "shell rendered" in ~210 ms instead of ~660 ms. Each layer is independently reviewable; the numbers below are for the whole stack.

| | PR | what |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | this | renderer boots the tick the window exists; entry chunk wires `oc://`, permissions, navigation, headers; shell gate values in argv |
| 2 | #50109 | main waits for the renderer's asset burst before evaluating its bundle |
| 3 | #50110 | renderer's initial module graph is one chunk |
| 4 | #50111 | crash reporter, onboarding scan, log cleanup, certs/proxy/netlog, CLI resolve, palette, service probe off the path |
| 5 | #50112 | renderer speaks the RPC wire format directly; Effect runtime out of its initial graph |
| 6 | #50113 | preload hands the window its persisted stores; first render is the hydrated one |
| 7 | #50114 | renderer CPU profiles attributed to source files (tooling) |

```mermaid
gantt
  dateFormat X
  axisFormat %L
  section before
  entry → ready               :a1, 0, 134
  window shown                :a2, 134, 192
  main bundle + layers        :a3, 192, 484
  renderer boot               :a4, 484, 583
  wait for port + 4 RPCs      :a5, 583, 889
  section after
  entry → ready               :b1, 0, 133
  window shown + loadURL      :b2, 133, 186
  renderer boot (main idle, serving assets) :b3, 186, 281
  main bundle + layers        :b4, 314, 448
  compile + evaluate + hydrated render :b5, 281, 390
```

This layer: `createEarlyWindow` registers the `oc://` handler, permissions, navigation policy and headers itself and calls `loadURL` in the same tick the window is created. The entry chunk stays Effect-free; the protocol handler reports through `console` until the logging layer installs a reporter. The window's argv carries `firstLaunchPending` and `defaultServerUrl` so the renderer can mount its shell without asking main; the locale is cached in `localStorage` for the same reason.

```ts
// main/index.ts
void app.whenReady().then(() => {
  createEarlyWindow()          // window + loadURL, before the main bundle is even imported
  return import("./desktop")
})
```

Packaged startup bench (`bun run bench:startup`), Windows laptop display, warm service, 5 interleaved runs, medians in ms since spawn, `v2` vs the full stack:

| | `v2` | stack |
|---|---|---|
| renderer process starts | 468 | **179** |
| DOM interactive | 582 | **263** |
| shell in DOM (titlebar tab) | 853 | **387** |
| composer editable | 853 | **613** |
| first pixels on screen | 573 | 622 |
| screen settled | 1132 | **945** |

Window → shell: **664 → 210 ms**. First pixels land ~50 ms later than before but as the complete hydrated frame; on stock Electron that instant is set by GPU shader compilation, which the renderer now finishes ahead of (electron/electron#54113 removes that wait).
